section_summary: This section documents U.S. efforts in mid-1941 to restrict petroleum and other strategic exports to Japan, including consultations with oil companies, the British and Dutch governments, and officials administering export controls and frozen Japanese funds. It also contains public and congressional complaints about continued oil shipments, reports on Japanese efforts to obtain Chilean copper and Bolivian rubber, and intelligence concerning Japanese trade pressure on Latin American countries. The closing documents address Japan's shortages of rubber and oil following American, British, Dutch, and Latin American restrictions.

subfiles.title: Envelope or routing cover for Gerald M. Fennell correspondence
subfiles.from: Gerald M. Fennell, The Navarro, New York
subfiles.about: Cover material records the delivery and routing of correspondence from Gerald M. Fennell to Sumner Welles.
subfiles.summary: The page bears The Navarro address, a July 12, 1941 date, and routing marks for the Department of State's Far Eastern Affairs office. It appears to have accompanied Fennell's correspondence concerning exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Gerald M. Fennell concerning oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary explains the legal and governmental basis for controlling petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter states that the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940 authorizes presidential restrictions on strategically important exports. It notes existing controls on aviation fuel, lubricants, and other petroleum products and says those controls apply to Japan. Welles adds that policy toward China and Japan is determined by the government as a whole and must account for many national and international considerations.

subfiles.title: Prentiss M. Brown forwards Dale O. Miller's criticism of exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Senator Brown forwards a constituent's response criticizing gasoline and aluminum shipments connected with Japan and Britain.
subfiles.summary: Brown refers to an earlier State Department reply about shipments of gasoline and aluminum to Japan. He encloses Dale O. Miller's July 14 letter and asks whether Welles wishes to comment, requesting that the enclosure be returned.

subfiles.title: Dale O. Miller to Senator Brown on oil and aluminum shipments
subfiles.about: Miller protests continued oil shipments to Japan and alleged inconsistencies in American and British aluminum policy.
subfiles.summary: Miller quotes a Detroit News report that Japanese vessels were loading more than 400,000 barrels of oil at Los Angeles Harbor. He contrasts these exports with calls for reduced domestic gasoline use and complains that British-made aluminum toys were entering the United States while American manufacturers lacked aluminum. He also alleges that Britain was supplying commercial and private aircraft to South America and questions the purpose of current policy.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Mr. Elkan concerning Chilean copper for Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains why a Chilean copper producer was allowed to sell part of its blister-copper output to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Elkan said M'Zaita needed outside ores as flux but faced Japanese bidding that made those purchases uneconomic. International Minerals & Metals Corporation therefore released 1,600 tons of annual blister-copper output for sale to Japan, enabling M'Zaita to avoid direct competition for ore and preserve most production for American or British sale. Preventing the Japanese transaction would reportedly require paying about $30 more per ton for the necessary ores.

subfiles.title: Advance confidential transmission on petroleum exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Green confidentially transmits advance copies of memoranda and statistics on petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green sends a July 19 memorandum addressed to Dean Acheson, its supporting documents, three statistical tables, and another memorandum. He explains that the formal memorandum to the Export Control Administrator is still under departmental consideration but will probably be approved and transmitted shortly.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to the July 17 Fennell reply
subfiles.about: The note cross-references the July 17 letter to Gerald M. Fennell.
subfiles.summary: This brief filing note identifies the letter to Gerald M. Fennell dated July 17, 1941. It connects the document to the relevant decimal-file entry.

subfiles.title: Gerald M. Fennell renews his protest against gasoline exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Fennell argues that American gasoline exports enable Japanese bombing in China and encloses supporting material.
subfiles.summary: Fennell thanks Welles for the July 17 reply but says it does not resolve his objection to supplying Japan with fuel. He forwards George A. Fitch's cable from Chongqing, invokes United China Relief's fundraising, and cites Japan's Axis ties and Hitler's request for Japanese aid. He also encloses images of Foreign Minister Teijiro Toyoda and Finance Minister Masatsune Ogura.

subfiles.title: Clipping: “Oil for Japan” and photographs of Japanese cabinet ministers
subfiles.from: Unidentified wife of George A. Fitch
subfiles.about: A published letter reproduces George A. Fitch's appeal for a stricter embargo on materials supporting Japanese bombing in China.
subfiles.summary: The clipping quotes Fitch's open cable to President Roosevelt describing deadly bombings in Chongqing, damage to American facilities, and danger to an American vessel. It argues that American gasoline and oil make Japan's attacks possible and calls for an end to such exports. The page also contains photographs identifying Teijiro Toyoda and Masatsune Ogura as members of the new Japanese cabinet.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of T. Y. Hill's letter
subfiles.about: A Senate form refers T. Y. Hill's enclosed letter to the State Department for consideration and report.
subfiles.summary: The referral asks the Department of State to give the enclosed communication favorable consideration as warranted. It requests a report to accompany the return of the enclosure.

subfiles.title: T. Y. Hill to Senator Connally opposing oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Hill urges an immediate end to oil sales and what he considers appeasement of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hill predicts that the United States will soon be at war with Japan and asks why Japanese tankers are still obtaining diesel fuel from California. He denounces Japan as likely to strike without warning and urges the United States to abandon appeasement in foreign and domestic affairs.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Connally about the Hill letter
subfiles.about: The Department points Senator Connally to the President's August 1 petroleum-export regulations.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Connally's August 25 transmission of T. Y. Hill's letter. It encloses the President's August 1 announcement of further petroleum-export regulations and suggests that Connally bring it to Hill's attention.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Minister in La Paz concerning Yungas rubber
subfiles.about: The Department asks the Legation to investigate possible Japanese efforts to obtain rubber from Bolivia's Yungas region.
subfiles.summary: The instruction transmits a British Embassy letter reporting Japanese interest in a Bolivian Yungas product believed to be rubber. The Department requests the Legation's attention and comments.

subfiles.title: British Embassy report on Japanese interest in Bolivian rubber
subfiles.about: Thorold reports that Japanese buyers are seeking samples of rubber from Bolivia's Yungas region.
subfiles.summary: Thorold identifies the Yungas as the forested rubber-producing region east of La Paz and notes that its rubber traditionally moved through Pará. He suggests that Japanese inquiries may indicate an attempt to bypass Brazilian export restrictions. Although likely quantities are small, he recommends considering the matter in negotiations with Bolivia over exports to undesirable destinations.

subfiles.title: Routing note concerning material left for Dean Acheson
subfiles.about: The note asks whether material left by Mr. Carr for Acheson still requires attention.
subfiles.summary: The writer says Mr. Carr left the material for Acheson to take home on Tuesday, August 5, and assumes it has been handled. The note asks that Alger Hiss be consulted to determine whether Acheson still needs to see it.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Standard-Vacuum representatives on petroleum shipments from the Netherlands East Indies
subfiles.about: Standard-Vacuum asks for formal U.S. guidance before seeking permits or accepting payment for oil shipments from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: George S. Walden and Mr. Singer said public criticism made the company unwilling to continue Japanese sales without government approval. They viewed the decision as a test of American policy and said the company would not seek Dutch export permits until the United States approved dollar transfers from Japanese interests. Stanley K. Hornbeck recommended postponing action for several days, although vessels were expected to begin loading by August 4.

subfiles.title: Routing request for approval of petroleum-policy memorandum
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: The note requests initials and routing approval for an attached memorandum.
subfiles.summary: The writer asks reviewers to initial the attached memorandum if it meets with their approval. Suggested routing includes the relevant geographic, political, and Far Eastern offices.

subfiles.title: Conversation with British and Dutch representatives on Netherlands East Indies petroleum
subfiles.about: American, British, and Dutch officials coordinate policy on applications and payments for petroleum shipments from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acheson proposed that Standard-Vacuum refrain from applying for export licenses under its Japanese contract and postpone applications for its ordinary quota business; Noel Hall agreed that Britain would take the same approach with Shell. Acheson told the Dutch representatives that the Indies government should decide freely whether exports would continue, while the United States would either license payment from blocked Japanese funds or refuse payment consistently with the Dutch decision. The Dutch representatives agreed to seek their government's views, and Acheson confidentially supplied details of current American petroleum restrictions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on sharing petroleum restrictions with Standard-Vacuum and Shell
subfiles.about: Hiss recommends confidentially sharing detailed American petroleum restrictions so Standard-Vacuum and Shell can apply comparable policies in the Indies.
subfiles.summary: Walden said Standard-Vacuum wanted its Netherlands East Indies shipments to be no more liberal than American exports to Japan, subject to Dutch approval. Hiss recommends giving Walden the same confidential material already supplied to Dutch and British representatives and permitting Noel Hall to share it with Shell. The suggested corporate policy would matter only if the Indies government did not itself adopt equally restrictive controls.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of the August 4 conversation on Netherlands East Indies petroleum
subfiles.about: This partial duplicate records the discussion with British and Dutch officials about restricting oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats Acheson's proposal that Standard-Vacuum and Shell refrain from making export-license applications and leave decisions to the Netherlands East Indies government. It also repeats the pledge that the United States would align licenses for payments from blocked Japanese funds with the Dutch decision. The surviving copy ends while describing the Dutch representatives' reaction and the temporary suspension of ordinary quota business.

subfiles.title: Recommendation concerning Standard-Vacuum's proposed 86-octane gasoline quotation
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green and Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes a carefully limited response to Standard-Vacuum about a possible export application for gasoline destined for Japanese forces in China.
subfiles.summary: The writer recommends telling A. G. May that the Department cannot advise the company on its proposed cable. It could say only that an application to export 86-octane gasoline to occupied China would receive the same consideration as comparable applications, with no assurance that existing licensing practice would continue. A handwritten note says May decided to take the chance and send the proposed telegram.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Standard-Vacuum concerning Japanese pressure in China
subfiles.about: Standard-Vacuum representatives describe Japanese military pressure to supply petroleum products, including 86-octane gasoline, in exchange for operating permits in China.
subfiles.summary: P. W. Parker and A. G. May said Japanese authorities threatened to withdraw shipping permissions and impose severe restrictions if the company refused the requested petroleum supplies. Parker feared that refusal could also lead to the commandeering of company storage facilities, especially if another firm supplied the gasoline. Officials privately disclosed that no licenses for 86-octane gasoline had recently been issued for Japan or occupied China, but would not promise to revoke older licenses. The memorandum notes that concern about public opinion in China and the United States strongly influenced the company's reluctance.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to F. J. Twogood concerning an 86-octane gasoline offer
subfiles.from: P. W. Parker or Standard-Vacuum headquarters
subfiles.about: The draft proposes quoting gasoline subject to an export permit and availability of a Japanese tanker.
subfiles.summary: The proposed reply says Standard-Vacuum is willing to quote 200,000 units of 86-octane gasoline ex West Coast. Any sale would depend on obtaining an export permit and chartering a full-cargo Japanese tanker through Shanghai, and the draft warns that the permit may be delayed.

subfiles.title: F. J. Twogood cable on Japanese demands and Shanghai shipping permits
subfiles.about: Twogood urges headquarters to reconsider refusing Japanese petroleum demands because the company's permits and position in China are at risk.
subfiles.summary: Twogood reports that permits for kerosene, diesel oil, and gasoline depend on the company's final response to Japanese demands. A favorable decision would bring shipping permits to Yangtze River points as far as Hankow, whereas refusal would jeopardize the company and Twogood personally. He urges an offer of some acceptable products, perhaps carried from the American West Coast in Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum cable refusing aviation oil and gasoline shipments
subfiles.from: P. W. Parker, Standard-Vacuum, New York
subfiles.about: Headquarters tells Twogood that supply conditions prevent offers or shipments of aviation oils or aviation-grade gasoline.
subfiles.summary: The cable acknowledges Twogood's earlier communication and notes that the State Department has not yet heard from the consulate. It states that Standard-Vacuum is unable, then or in the near future, to offer aviation oils or gasoline recommended for aviation use.

subfiles.title: O. C. Brewster to Max Thornburg on petroleum quotas for Japan
subfiles.about: Brewster asks Thornburg to confirm a meeting's conclusion that Japan could obtain its permitted quotas of non-embargoed crude oil and gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Brewster recalls a consensus that Japan would have little difficulty obtaining the quota quantities of crude oil and non-embargoed gasoline and that the gasoline would be suitable for civilian motor fuel. Thornburg's annotation essentially agrees, while allowing that Japan might encounter some difficulty.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum with the Commercial Attaché at Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Collado discusses Japanese bunker supplies, immobilized ships, and British ship warrants with Walter J. Donnelly in Rio de Janeiro.
subfiles.summary: Donnelly says Brazil is following the American policy of giving Japanese vessels only enough bunker fuel to reach their ports, while Collado stresses hemisphere defense needs. They also discuss plans for immobilized ships and the German vessel Nordnerney, which lacked assurance of safe passage from Britain. Collado objects to British control of Western Hemisphere, especially coastwise, shipping through ship warrants.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with George S. Walden on the effect of petroleum specifications
subfiles.about: Walden reports that American petroleum specifications would bar nearly all crude oil and gasoline exports from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Walden says only special Tarakan crude, effectively a natural diesel oil, could meet the American rules, and he believes no gasoline then made in the Indies would qualify. After hearing of a message from van Karnebeek indicating that crude exports would not be allowed, he postpones cabling his representatives. He asks for a prompt decision on Netherlands Indies policy so the company can make arrangements.

subfiles.title: Confidential report on letters of credit for diesel oil
subfiles.about: Hoover reports two Shanghai-issued letters of credit for diesel-oil purchases in the United States that might be reshipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source reported that the Bank of Canton's San Francisco branch held two letters of credit issued in Shanghai for diesel-oil purchases. One covered 2,000 tons from the American Petroleum Export Company in Los Angeles; the other covered 1,200 tons from a San Francisco beneficiary. The source believed the oil might ultimately be sent to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on information about phosphate exports
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to an original document containing information about phosphate exports.
subfiles.summary: The page is a largely blank cross-reference form. Its subject is information concerning exports of phosphates, but the originating document and file details are not legible or were not completed.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Welles memorandum on oil exports and Japanese access to Netherlands East Indies oil
subfiles.about: The sheet references a confidential Welles memorandum about oil-export restrictions discussed with the Japanese ambassador.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum concerned a conversation between the President and the Japanese ambassador about restricted American oil exports. It also addressed Japanese activity in the Netherlands East Indies intended to secure a larger oil supply. The original was filed under number 711.94/2177.

subfiles.title: Welles instructions for freezing funds and tightening trade controls
subfiles.about: Welles requests papers to implement asset freezes, possible silk-import restrictions, and tighter petroleum-export standards for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles calls for simultaneous freezing of Japanese and Chinese funds and consideration of restrictions on silk and other imports from Japan. He also requests lower permitted octane and lubricant specifications and petroleum quotas based on a normal export period. He wants the necessary papers ready by Monday.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Petroleum Schedule No. 10 classifications
subfiles.about: Brewster explains API-gravity reporting and commodity classifications for petroleum export applications under Schedule No. 10.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says exporters should report API gravity for each item, using a range when a single entry covers mixed products. It distinguishes newly controlled products eligible for general licenses from products already requiring individual licenses. It also explains how aviation fuels, lubricants, natural gasoline, petroleum coke, and related commodities must be separated on applications.

subfiles.title: Table of United States petroleum-product exports, 1935–1936
subfiles.about: The table presents annual and average export quantities for numerous petroleum products in 1935 and 1936.
subfiles.summary: The categories include crude petroleum, gasoline, gas and fuel oils, residual fuel oil, lubricants, kerosene, transformer oil, greases, asphalt, petroleum coke, petroleum jelly, paraffin wax, and liquefied petroleum gases. Quantities are expressed in barrels, tons, or pounds, with averages for the two years.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Coordinator referral of Charles P. Copeland's letter
subfiles.about: Holland refers Copeland's complaint about petroleum exports to the State Department for consideration and reply.
subfiles.summary: Holland explains that petroleum-export matters fall within the jurisdiction of the Department of State. He therefore forwards the attached letter to Secretary Hull for handling.

subfiles.title: Charles P. Copeland to Harold Ickes protesting exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Copeland objects to gasoline conservation at home while petroleum and other war materials allegedly continue to go to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Copeland asks whether Americans are being asked to reduce Sunday driving so oil companies can keep selling gasoline to Japan. He argues that Japanese reserves could be used against the United States and also condemns earlier scrap-iron exports that aided Japan's war in China. He urges reliance on substitutes for Japanese silk rather than continued trade.

subfiles.title: La Paz despatch on Japanese efforts to obtain Yungas rubber
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, United States Legation at La Paz
subfiles.about: The Legation reports its investigation of alleged Japanese plans to buy and ship Bolivian and Pará rubber.
subfiles.summary: British information indicated that Nabei, Mitsui's Buenos Aires agent, had been asked from Santiago to book space aboard Buenos Aires Maru for forty tons of Pará rubber. Proceso Kuto was reportedly authorized to buy the rubber, determine monthly Yungas availability, and send samples to Buenos Aires and Tokyo. Neither the British nor American legation could confirm Kuto's presence or Japanese purchasing activity in Bolivia, but further inquiries were promised.

subfiles.title: Finletter reports La Paz findings to the British Embassy
subfiles.about: Finletter relays the American Legation's findings on suspected Japanese purchases of Bolivian and Pará rubber.
subfiles.summary: The letter quotes the La Paz report concerning Nabei, Proceso Kuto, the Buenos Aires Maru, and requests for rubber samples. It notes that neither legation had verified Kuto's activities or found evidence of Japanese attempts to purchase rubber in Bolivia. The American Legation would continue investigating.

subfiles.title: Senator Barbour forwards inquiry about oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Barbour asks the State Department for information to answer John J. Flaherty, Jr. about whether American oil is being sold to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The senator encloses a letter from Jersey City attorney John J. Flaherty, Jr. He requests the Department's views so that he can give Flaherty an informed answer.

subfiles.title: John J. Flaherty, Jr. reports a motor-oil shipment to Japan
subfiles.about: Flaherty reports an alleged Bayway shipment of aviation motor oil to Yokohama and asks that the information aid Chinese efforts to stop such exports.
subfiles.summary: Flaherty says the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey was preparing a large shipment of aviation motor oil from its Bayway plant for export to Japan through Yokohama. He notes unusual instructions against placing the consignee's name on the packages and says he passed the information to British and federal investigators. He argues that it is unjust to aid China while allowing materials useful to Japan's military to be exported.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Barbour
subfiles.about: The Department answers Barbour by citing the President's August 1 petroleum-export regulations.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Barbour's transmission of John J. Flaherty's letter about oil exports to Japan. It encloses the August 1 presidential announcement and notes that Flaherty's March letter predated the new regulations.

subfiles.title: Senator McNary forwards H. D. Willits's inquiry
subfiles.about: McNary requests information in response to a constituent asking about sales of oil and military supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McNary encloses H. D. Willits's inquiry and asks the State Department to provide whatever information is available. He also asks that the enclosure be returned with the reply.

subfiles.title: H. D. Willits postcard asking about military exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Willits asks whether the United States is still selling oil or other military supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief postcard asks Senator McNary to determine whether American oil or other military supplies are currently being sold to Japan. Willits supplies his Portland address.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator McNary
subfiles.about: The Department summarizes current restrictions on petroleum and other militarily significant exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply says exports of high-grade gasoline and lubricating oils are prohibited except to the Western Hemisphere, the British Empire, and unoccupied territories resisting aggression. Low-grade petroleum exports to other destinations have been severely curtailed, and similar restrictions cover other commodities of military significance. Willits's communication is returned.

subfiles.title: Noel Hall proposes joint study of Japan's oil supplies
subfiles.about: Hall proposes a small Anglo-American group to examine Japan's petroleum stocks, tanker access, ship warrants, and bunker controls.
subfiles.summary: Hall suggests studying Japanese oil requirements, the effect of withdrawing non-Japanese tankers, and indirect pressure through ship warrants and bunker control. He reports discussing the proposal with Max Thornburg and Eric Wyndham-White. Hall emphasizes the need for close coordination between British and American administrative arrangements.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Coordinator referral of alleged diesel-oil shipment
subfiles.about: Holland refers correspondence about an alleged diesel-oil shipment to Japan to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Holland encloses Senator C. Wayland Brooks's letter, T. A. Shaw's complaint, and the Petroleum Coordinator's reply. He explains that export control and licensing fall under State Department jurisdiction and refers the matter for any desired action.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Holland's referral on alleged diesel-oil shipment
subfiles.about: This duplicate forwards the Brooks and Shaw correspondence about an alleged diesel-oil shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats that export control and licensing are State Department responsibilities. It refers the enclosed correspondence for whatever action the Department considers appropriate.

subfiles.title: Holland replies to Senator Brooks
subfiles.about: Holland tells Brooks that the alleged Japanese diesel-oil shipment has been referred to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Holland acknowledges Brooks's August 19 letter and T. A. Shaw's enclosed complaint. He apologizes for the delay and explains that the newly created Petroleum Coordinator's office faces a heavy workload. Copies have been sent to the State Department, and Shaw's original letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Senator Brooks forwards T. A. Shaw's complaint
subfiles.about: Brooks forwards a constituent's letter and newspaper clipping about diesel oil allegedly being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brooks submits T. A. Shaw's letter and an August 12 Chicago Tribune clipping for Ickes's attention. He asks for information that he can transmit to Shaw.

subfiles.title: T. A. Shaw protests diesel-oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Shaw asks why the United States is selling diesel oil to Japan when it is needed domestically.
subfiles.summary: Referring to an attached Chicago Tribune clipping, Shaw contends that diesel oil is needed in the United States for refining into gasoline and other products. He asks Senator Brooks to investigate why such sales are being allowed.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Brooks
subfiles.about: Hull explains that earlier oil exports were intended to preserve peace and points to the August 1 petroleum regulations.
subfiles.summary: The reply says President Roosevelt had explained in July that previous oil exports to Japan were permitted in the hope of preserving peace in the Pacific. It encloses the August 1 announcement of new national-defense regulations governing all petroleum products. Brooks is invited to bring the announcement to Shaw's attention.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Tokyo on Japanese trade reprisals in Latin America
subfiles.about: The Department requests information about Japanese attempts to force Latin American countries to supply strategic materials through trade retaliation.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports that Japan stopped supplying rayon to Mexico after Mexico withheld minerals and threatened similar action against Brazilian textile interests. It asks the Embassy to report Japanese efforts to induce Latin American republics to provide minerals or other defense materials by comparable reprisals.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese silk and rayon reprisals against Mexico and Colombia
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Japanese use of silk and rayon exports as leverage for Mexican minerals and Colombian platinum.
subfiles.summary: Japan reportedly cancelled licenses for silk and rayon destined for Mexico because Mexico refused to export strategic minerals. American officials were attempting to find a United States rayon supply for Mexico. The Embassy in Colombia separately reported that Japan conditioned silk sales on access to Colombian platinum.

subfiles.title: Tokyo report on Japanese trade reprisals against Latin America
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports limited evidence of Japanese trade reprisals and declining Japanese commerce with Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Latin American representatives in Tokyo knew of no additional reprisals beyond the Mexican rayon cutoff and a stopped Colombian silk shipment. They were not greatly alarmed because reduced shipping, American raw-material purchases, and hemispheric export restrictions had already diminished trade with Japan. Peru reportedly welcomed the loss of Japanese textiles because they had competed with domestic producers; information from Chilean and Brazilian representatives was still pending.

subfiles.title: Tokyo report on Japan's rubber shortage and Dutch export policy
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports Japan's worsening rubber shortage and the Netherlands' refusal to release strategic materials from the East Indies.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese Foreign Office official said hopes for rubber supplies from Indochina and Thailand had failed, making the Netherlands East Indies vital. He asserted that American rubber stocks exceeded 800,000 tons, but a Dutch official replied that materials potentially usable against the Netherlands and its allies could not be exported to Japan. Four Japanese tankers were reportedly still waiting for oil in Netherlands East Indies waters after the freezing order.

subfiles.title: State Department correction of Japanese claims about United States rubber stocks
subfiles.about: The Department supplies accurate American rubber-stock figures and explains why continued accumulation is essential.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that total American rubber stocks on July 31 were 395,216 tons, divided among industry, the Rubber Reserve, and deliveries under the British cotton-rubber barter agreement. Stocks were rising because priorities had curtailed deliveries to manufacturers, but reaching 800,000 tons would still require roughly eight months at the current rate. The Department emphasizes that defense production and stockpile accumulation justify continued American purchasing and allows the Commercial Attaché to discuss the figures confidentially with his Dutch colleague.
